items.title: Concentration and Wisdom Complete: All Fifty-One Verses on the Three Trainings Close (continued)

items.zh: 於學到究竟，善斷諸疑網，今請學所學，修學為我說」者，於此頌中，大梵天王先讚世尊，後興請問。讚世尊者，謂於一切學中，已得第一究竟。此依自利行圓滿不共德說；又能善斷展轉所生一切疑網，此依利他行圓滿不共德說。興請問者，何等為學？學有幾種？云何於彼當修學耶？
items.en: 'You have reached the ultimate in training and have well cut the net of doubts; I now ask about training and what is to be trained: please explain to me how to train.' In this verse the great Brahmā King first praises the World-Honoured One and then asks his question. In praising the World-Honoured One, he says that in all training he has reached the foremost ultimate; this refers to the unique quality of having fulfilled the practice of benefiting oneself. And he has well cut all the net of doubts that arise one after another; this refers to the unique quality of having fulfilled the practice of benefiting others. In asking his question, he asks: What is training? How many kinds of training are there? How should one train in them?

items.title: Why Just Three Trainings: The Prose Commentary's Opening Rationale

items.zh: 是故世尊意為策勵怖多所作懈怠眾生，總攝一切，略說三學。故次告曰：大仙應善聽！學略有三種：增上戒、心、慧。於彼當修學。
items.en: For this reason, the Blessed One's intent was to encourage beings who, dreading how much there is to accomplish, grow lazy and discouraged — and so he gathered everything to be learned together, and taught it concisely as three trainings.

items.zh: 此中顯示依戒、心、慧，若散亂者，令不散亂，方便為說增上戒學；心未定者，為令得定，方便為說增上心學；心已得定未解脫者，為令解脫，方便為說增上慧學。由此因緣，諸修行者一切所作皆得究竟。
items.en: This shows that, resting on precepts, mind, and wisdom: for one who is scattered, so that they become unscattered, the higher training in precepts is taught as the skilful means; for one whose mind is not yet settled, so that it becomes settled, the higher training in mind is taught as the skilful means; and for one whose mind is settled but not yet liberated, so that they become liberated, the higher training in wisdom is taught as the skilful means. By this cause, every practitioner's entire task reaches its culmination.

items.zh: 此顯世尊密意宣說一切諸學，無不攝在此三學中。又為顯示於諸學中，由此方便成辦所學，故次說言：應圓滿六支，四樂住成就，於四各四行，智慧常清淨。今此頌中，如其次第，顯示成辦三學方便。應圓滿六支者，應依增上戒學方便修學。何等六支？一、安住淨尸羅，二、守護別解脫律儀，三、軌則圓滿，四、所行圓滿，五、於諸小罪見大怖畏，六、受學學處。如是六支，顯示四種尸羅清淨。安住淨尸羅者，是所依根本。守護別解脫律儀者，顯示出離尸羅清淨，為求解脫而出離故。軌則、所行俱圓滿者，此二顯示無所譏毀尸羅清淨。於諸小罪見大怖畏者，顯無穿缺尸羅清淨。受學學處者，顯無顛倒尸羅清淨。如是六支極圓滿故，增上戒學與餘方便作所依止。四樂住成就者，顯示增上心學方便。四種靜慮，名四心住；現法樂住，故名為樂。於四各四行，智慧常清淨者，依增上慧學說。謂於苦集滅道四聖諦中，一一皆有四行。即無常等。增上慧學由此淨智之所顯故。「初善住根本，次樂心寂靜，後聖見惡見，相應不相應」者，此頌顯示增上三學次第生起。根本者，謂增上戒。由後二種是此初學所流類故。既具尸羅，由無悔等次第修習，能得第二心樂靜定。心得定者，見如實故，能得第三成就聖見，遠離惡見。「先淨樂靜慮，及於諦善巧，即於諸諦中，應生、遠、增長」者，此頌顯示三學次第清淨差別。先淨者，是初學。樂靜慮者，是第二學。於諦善巧者，是第三學。又於如是諦善巧中，應生者，謂道諦。應生起故。應遠者，謂苦、集諦。應遠離故。應增長者，謂滅諦。軟中上品煩惱次第數數漸斷，增長滅故。「於諸學處中，有四趣三所。遠離於二趣，於二趣證得」者，此頌顯示於增上戒心慧學處，由所修學有成敗故，隨其所應，所得果報四趣差別。謂於欲界人天所攝所有善趣，是增上戒成所得果；即於欲界餘趣所攝所有惡趣，是增上戒敗所得果。色無色界天趣所攝所有上趣，是增上心果。三界所不攝涅槃趣，是增上慧果。於如是諸趣中、遠離前二善趣、惡趣已，應證後二上趣及涅槃趣。此言顯示世出世間二道所得。「二安住二種，一能趣涅槃，漸次為因緣，純雜而修習」者，於此頌中，顯示最初增上戒學、增上心學，漸次能為增上心學、增上慧學安住因緣。顯示中間增上慧、靜慮律儀所攝增上戒學，能為二種安住因緣。顯示最上一種，能為涅槃安住因緣。當知此中顯示修習若別若總，隨其所應。
items.en: This shows the World-Honoured One's hidden intention in teaching that all trainings are included in these three trainings. Further, to show the means by which, within the trainings, what is to be trained is accomplished, the next verse says: 'Fulfil the six limbs; accomplish the four abidings in joy; in each of the four, four aspects; wisdom always pure.' This verse shows, in order, the means of accomplishing the three trainings. 'Fulfil the six limbs' means one should train by relying on the means of the training in higher ethics. What are the six limbs? First, abiding in pure ethics; second, guarding the prātimokṣa restraint; third, being complete in deportment; fourth, being complete in where one goes; fifth, seeing great danger in the slightest faults; sixth, taking up and training in the precepts. These six limbs show four kinds of purity of ethics. Abiding in pure ethics is the basic support. Guarding the prātimokṣa restraint shows the purity of ethics of renunciation, because one renounces in order to seek liberation. Being complete in deportment and in where one goes shows the purity of ethics that is beyond reproach. Seeing great danger in the slightest faults shows the purity of ethics that is without breach. Taking up and training in the precepts shows the purity of ethics that is without distortion. Because these six limbs are fully complete, the training in higher ethics serves as the support for the other means. 'Accomplish the four abidings in joy' shows the means of the training in higher mind. The four dhyānas are called the four abidings of mind; because they are abiding in happiness in this present life, they are called joy. 'In each of the four, four aspects; wisdom always pure' refers to the training in higher wisdom: in each of the four noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and path there are four aspects, impermanence and the rest; the training in higher wisdom is shown by this pure knowledge. 'First, rest well in the root; next, delight in a calm mind; last, noble view and evil view, associated and not associated': this verse shows the order in which the three higher trainings arise. The root is higher ethics, because the latter two flow from this first training. Having ethics complete, and cultivating in order through freedom from regret and the rest, one can attain the second, the mind's joyful, calm concentration. When the mind is concentrated, one sees as it really is, and so can attain the third, accomplishing noble view and leaving evil view behind. 'First purity, joy in dhyāna, and skill in the truths; within the truths, what should be produced, left behind, and increased': this verse shows the differences in purity of the three trainings in order. 'First purity' is the first training; 'joy in dhyāna' is the second; 'skill in the truths' is the third. Further, within this skill in the truths, 'what should be produced' is the truth of the path, because it should be made to arise; 'what should be left behind' is the truths of suffering and origination, because they should be left behind; 'what should be increased' is the truth of cessation, because, as mild, middling, and strong afflictions are cut off step by step and repeatedly, cessation increases. 'Within the trainings there are four destinies and three places; leaving two destinies behind, one realises two destinies': this verse shows that, in the trainings in higher ethics, mind, and wisdom, according to whether what is trained succeeds or fails, the resulting fruits differ as four destinies. The good destinies included in humans and gods of the desire realm are the fruit of success in higher ethics; the bad destinies included in the other destinies of the desire realm are the fruit of failure in higher ethics. The higher destinies included in the gods of the form and formless realms are the fruit of higher mind. The destiny of nirvana, not included in the three realms, is the fruit of higher wisdom. Among these destinies, having left behind the first two, the good and bad destinies, one should realise the latter two, the higher destinies and the destiny of nirvana. This shows what is attained by the worldly and the world-transcending paths. 'Two are abidings for two; one leads to nirvana; step by step they are causes and conditions; cultivate them singly and together': this verse shows that the first, the training in higher ethics, and the training in higher mind can step by step be the causes and conditions for abiding in the training in higher mind and in higher wisdom. It shows that the middle, the training in higher ethics included in the restraint of higher wisdom and of dhyāna, can be the cause and condition of the two abidings. It shows that the highest one can be the cause and condition of abiding in nirvana. It should be understood that this shows cultivation, singly or together, as appropriate.

blocks.text: The treatise now explains the fifty-one verses in prose. Ru-Yi translates only two passages (0367a13–a19); **the rest of today's Chinese is missing from Ru-Yi's translation** (0367a06–a12 and from 0367a20), and the English column gives our own translation. The commentary summarises it, verse by verse. It explains the verses you read on Day 132.

In the opening verse, Brahmā first praises the Buddha, then asks. "Reached the culmination of training" is the Buddha's own perfection (self-benefit); "cut through every net of doubt", his benefit to others. Master Cháng Bǎi: this "doesn't mean the Buddha practises for beings to cut their doubts", but that the scriptures he taught do so. Brahmā asks three things: what training is, how many kinds, and how to train.

(Translated.) The Buddha taught briefly, as three trainings, to encourage beings who "dread how much there is to accomplish" and so grow lazy. Master Cháng Bǎi: told that three countless aeons of diligence are needed, they lose heart. Precepts calm the scattered, concentration settles the unsettled, and wisdom frees the settled mind. Master Cháng Bǎi on the last: concentration alone is "just a stone pressing on grass", keeping afflictions from showing for a while; it cannot liberate.

items: **Six supports, four purities.** The six supports are: abiding in pure moral discipline; guarding the prātimokṣa; perfect deportment; perfect conduct; seeing great danger in the slightest faults; and undertaking the rules of training. They show four kinds of purity: of renunciation (guarding the vows in order to seek liberation), of being beyond reproach (deportment and conduct), of being without breach (fearing slight faults), and of being without distortion (undertaking the rules). The first is the basis.
**Mind and wisdom.** The four dhyānas are the "four abidings of mind", "blissful" because they are a pleasant abiding here and now. Wisdom is the sixteen aspects of the four truths.

**Order and purity.** Precepts are the root because the other two flow from them: having moral discipline, one has no remorse, and so on, until the mind settles; a settled mind sees as it is. "Should arise" is the path; "should be left" are suffering and its origin; "should increase" is cessation, as afflictions are cut by degrees.

**Four destinations.** Good and bad destinies within the desire realm are the results of keeping or breaking precepts; the higher realms, of concentration; nirvāṇa, of wisdom. The first two are mundane, the last two the fruits of the mundane and supramundane paths.
**Two abidings.** The first two trainings are the basis for higher mind and higher wisdom; precepts included in meditation and wisdom underlie the two; the highest training is the basis for nirvāṇa.

blocks.text: The prose is quiet and technical, but its point is pastoral. The Buddha did not give an endless list. He gave three things, in order, each resting on the one before. Venerable Miào Jìng: gather all learning into three, and mastering these completes it.

quiz.q: Brahmā praises the Buddha as "skilfully cutting every net of doubt." Does this mean the Buddha cuts doubts for beings, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: no — the Buddha doesn't practice for beings; the teachings he spoke help them cut doubt
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Skilfully cutting nets of doubt doesn't mean the Buddha practices for beings to cut their doubts, but the sutras, Vinaya, and treatises he spoke." Reaching the culmination is self-benefit; cutting doubt, other-benefit.

quiz.q: The prose says the Buddha taught three trainings for beings "dreading how much there is to do." What do they dread, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: hearing that three countless eons of tireless diligence are needed, they grow afraid and unwilling to endure it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: told that three countless eons of tireless diligence are required, they become afraid and unwilling to bear such hardship. Venerable Miào Jìng: gather all learning into three, and mastering these completes it.

quiz.q: "For one settled but not yet liberated, the higher training in wisdom." What does Master Cháng Bǎi say of concentration alone?
options: like a stone pressing grass — affliction is only temporarily suppressed; such concentration cannot liberate
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "It's just a stone pressing on grass, keeping afflictions from manifesting for a while. Such concentration cannot liberate." The *Pixunji* lists eight tasks as "every task."
